tells: Plain report of the Sheikh's reading with 'he says' woven in mid-sentence, short declaratives and a gloss on the quotation ('He means this as a statement of what we were made for'), as in the reference's 'In most of us, he says, it is not working.'

Opens by picking up the previous argument (faculty, repair, more than the minimum) in short plain sentences; the colon-list of examples follows the reference's 'in marriage, in the people we meet, in sleep...' pattern.

'If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works' picks up the last step exactly as the reference's 'If the signs are present and plain...'; ends on a plain one-line lead into the next verse.
'Most of us fear Allah's punishment. The people of this verse fear Him...' mirrors 'Most of us see only the lamp'; verses introduced by a plain sentence saying what they describe.
Short defining sentences, a concrete everyday example (hunger, anxiety) and the Sheikh's view attributed in passing ('the Sheikh notes'), with no flourish at the end.

'Turning spoken lectures into a book has called for some editorial adaptation' — abstract, corporate diction; Author A would say plainly what was changed, e.g. 'The lectures have been reordered and edited.'
'To suit a wider readership, the book also adds context and explanation to support its main arguments' — blurb register; Author A names the thing directly rather than 'support its main arguments'.
'This book is inspired by a lecture series' — promotional 'inspired by'; Author A would write 'This book is based on'.

Each scholar's view reported then glossed in a plain closing sentence ('In his scheme, what is learned from the jurist begins the circle'; 'His list starts with the heart...'), as the reference glosses Tabatabaʾi's red light.

Short topic sentence leading into the quotation ('The second request is love'), then the Sheikh's reading laid out in two parts and tied back to an earlier chapter, as the reference does with 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.'

Quotation unpacked in the next sentence; 'It might seem to follow... Sheikh Bahmanpour does not draw that conclusion' is the reference's habit of stating a possible inference and then correcting it plainly.
'remain an ongoing conversation among our ʿulamaʾ' — abstract, journalistic cliche; Author A would write 'our ʿulamaʾ differ on'.
'this book presents each view with neutrality' — stiff nominalisation; Author A would write 'this book gives each view'.
'Three guiding principles frame the discussions in the chapters that follow' — grand, abstract framing; Author A states the point first ('Three things hold throughout the book').
'is explored in Chapter Nine' — stock signposting; Author A says what a chapter shows ('Chapter Nine shows how...').
'asks why a believer should bother' — informal, spoken 'bother'; Author A would write 'why a believer should go beyond the minimum'.
'with the goal of ʿirfan already on our lips in our duʿas' — figurative idiom layered on a literal phrase; Author A would write 'already asked for in the duʿas we recite'.
'with a compatible view of similarities to Sufism' — muddled abstract phrasing; Author A would state the relation plainly ('and how it differs from Sufism').

'Requests like this one were written for us, by the Imams (as), as an endeavour for the ordinary believer' — odd grand diction ('as an endeavour'); Author A would write 'The Imams (as) wrote requests like this for ordinary believers to say.'
'Despite saying these words in our munajats and on auspicious occasions, we find that...' — wordy 'Despite... we find' opening; Author A would write 'We say these words often, yet...'
'are the dominant undertaking' and 'is often less practised' — abstract, academic register; Author A would write 'are what we do' / 'we rarely practise'.
Sheikh's account reported plainly with a short quotation spoken to, tied back to Chapter One's 'rusted faculty', and a one-line lead into the next prayer.
Scholars cited in turn with quotations folded into the sentence, then a short paragraph setting their emphases side by side, as the reference sets Bahmanpour, Shomali and Khomeini beside each other.
Short balancing sentences ('The scholars speak of...; the Sheikh speaks of...') and a paragraph that opens by picking up the last phrase ('Access to these words...'), as in the reference's linking.

Each verse introduced by a plain sentence saying what it promises, then the Sheikh's reading; 'None of this would matter... Surah al-Nisaʾ answers that concern' matches the reference's 'The Qur'an says where it lies.'
'details some of the words you'll meet' — direct 'you' and a contraction; Author A uses 'we/us' or third person and no contractions.
'a welcoming introduction to ʿirfan, a guide to beginning the journey that strives for brevity and clarity' — promotional self-description; Author A never praises the book's own qualities.
'Additional call-out sections are spread throughout with helpful context and short side notes' — brochure register; Author A would write 'Boxes give background along the way.'
'And it ends not in withdrawal' — sentence opening on 'And'; Author A would join it to the previous sentence.
Plain definitional opening, contrast drawn in short sentences, quotations attributed in the sentence ('in Sheikh Bahmanpour's words') and tied back to the Munajat.
